reason: The sources provide ample, highly detailed, and cross-verified accounts of the Skylab 4 mission, the rookie crew, their workload disputes, and the truth behind the rumored space strike.
story: In 1973, NASA launched Skylab 4, its final mission to America's first space station. The crew—Gerald Carr, Edward Gibson, and William Pogue—were all space rookies facing an incredibly dense and demanding 84-day schedule. Tensions with mission control began early when the astronauts tried to hide Pogue's space sickness, only to be caught via onboard recordings and reprimanded. As the crushing workload wore them down, they decided to rotate who attended daily briefings. But one day, due to an accidental radio oversight, they missed a briefing entirely, resulting in a 90-minute communications blackout. The media sensationalized this accident as a deliberate 'strike in space.' In reality, the crew and ground control held a radio 'sensitivity session' on December 30 to ease the schedule. The compromise worked: the relaxed crew went on to set massive productivity records, proving that micromanagement fails even in orbit. Yet, none of the three astronauts ever flew in space again.
angle: The famous 'mutiny in space' where astronauts supposedly went on strike and cut off contact with NASA was actually an accidental 90-minute radio mistake by an exhausted, overworked crew.

claims.claim: Skylab was the first space station operated by the United States.
Skylab 4 was the third and final crewed mission to the Skylab space station.
The Skylab 4 crew consisted of Gerald Carr, Edward Gibson, and William Pogue.
All three members of the Skylab 4 crew were space rookies on their first flight.
The Skylab 4 mission launched on November 16, 1973, and lasted for 84 days.
Upon arriving at the station, the crew found three dummies dressed in flight suits left as a prank by the previous crew.
Pilot William Pogue suffered from space sickness shortly after reaching orbit.
The crew tried to hide Pogue's space sickness from mission control, but NASA discovered it via recorded onboard conversations.
NASA's chief of the astronaut office, Alan Shepard, reprimanded the crew for hiding the space sickness.
The crew struggled and became heavily fatigued due to an extremely dense and micromanaged work schedule.
An accidental radio error caused the crew to miss a scheduled daily briefing, resulting in a 90-minute communications gap with ground control.
The media and subsequent reports sensationalized this brief communication gap as a deliberate 'strike' or 'mutiny' in space.
NASA, historians, and the astronauts have all denied that a deliberate strike or mutiny took place.
On December 30, 1973, the crew and ground control held an air-to-ground radio conference to resolve scheduling tensions and lighten the workload.
After their schedule was relaxed, the crew's productivity rose significantly, and they completed more work than originally planned.
None of the three Skylab 4 astronauts ever flew in space again.
The Skylab space station's orbit decayed, and it fell to Earth in 1979.

disputed: The exact publication date of the New Yorker article containing the strike claim is disputed (S1 states August 22, 1976, while S2 states August 30, 1976). The script should refer to it generally as an August 1976 article.

The exact cause of the 90-minute silence is described differently (S1 claims they forgot to turn on their radios, while S3 and S7 state they got their signals crossed). The script should attribute it to an accidental communications error rather than choosing one specific cause.
